row.note: Jacob calls his sons to hear what will happen to them; the commentary reads mutual counsel as a word handed on at the edge of death, while its cited Qur'anic Jacob asks specifically whom they will worship.
As death approaches Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers; it joins a dying instruction, an heir and a binding oath in one scene.
Dying Joseph makes Israel's sons swear to carry his bones away when God visits them; an obligation is entrusted to a later generation.
God chooses Abraham so he will command his children and household after him to keep the Lord's way by doing righteousness and justice; faith and right conduct are transmitted together.

Jacob orders his household to put away foreign gods and purify themselves; this supplies an earlier concrete worship instruction beside the commentary's deathbed question about what his sons will worship.
Israel is told to repeat the commanded words to its children in daily settings; counsel becomes a continuing intergenerational duty like the commentary's inherited recommendation.
God establishes testimony in Jacob and commands fathers to make it known to their children; the commentary's passed-on faith has a precise communal analogue.

row.basis: children yet unborn tell their children
row.note: The next generation is to arise and tell its own children; this explicitly extends the chain beyond the first recipients of the bequest.
When David's death draws near he gives Solomon a charge; this is a royal deathbed instance of instruction left to someone who must act after the speaker.
David tells Solomon to keep God's charge and walk in his ways; the inherited instruction has religious practice, rather than property alone, as its subject.

row.basis: Moses warns what follows his death
row.note: Moses says Israel will turn aside after his death, making the survival of a transmitted charge after the speaker's absence the explicit issue.
A person gives a neighbor silver or goods for safekeeping and the goods are stolen; this is the concrete entrusted property behind the commentary's emanet image. This is WLC verse 22:6.
If the thief is not found, the householder must come before God about the neighbor's property; custody creates accountable testimony, as in the commentary's deathbed trust.
An oath of the Lord settles whether the keeper has touched the owner's animal, and the owner accepts it; entrusted goods and an oath share a single legal scene. This is WLC verse 22:10.

row.basis: two or three witnesses establish a matter
row.note: A single witness cannot establish a charge, whereas two or three can; it gives legal weight to the commentary's pair of witnesses at a bequest.
Judges must examine testimony carefully and determine whether a witness lied; this matches the commentary's concern that a first bequest testimony may prove deceptive.
The false witness receives the consequence intended for the accused; the commentary's replacement oath likewise treats corrupt testimony as a wrong requiring correction.
A person who hears an adjuration and can testify but fails to tell what was seen or known bears guilt; oath and the duty to disclose meet in the commentary's witness scene.
A person accused by a neighbor comes to swear before God's altar; the commentary likewise places a disputed oath after communal worship.
Solomon asks God to judge the sworn dispute and vindicate the righteous; this specifies the concern for a truer testimony when a first oath is suspect.
God declares Zelophehad's daughters' claim right and commands their father's inheritance be transferred to them; the commentary treats heirs' portions as enforceable rights.

The inheritance sequence ends by making its order a fixed statute of judgment; Hebrew חֻקַּת from the table's חקק correspondence links prescribed law to the commentary's binding haqq, without equating the two senses.

row.basis: father may not redirect firstborn status
row.note: A father with loved and unloved wives cannot favor the loved wife's son when allocating his estate; the bequest must respect a preexisting heir's right.
The father must recognize the unloved wife's firstborn with a double share; this concretizes a binding inheritance portion despite personal preference.

row.basis: prince's gift to son becomes inheritance
row.note: When the prince gives from his property to a son, it belongs to his sons as inherited possession; this tests the commentary's image of a father's gift and heirs' rights.

row.basis: gift to servant reverts at release
row.note: A prince's gift to a servant reverts to the prince at the year of liberty, while the son's inheritance in the preceding verse persists; it sharply qualifies the commentary's father who takes back a gift.
Judah personally stands surety for Benjamin and offers to bear blame if he fails to return him; the Genesis Joseph story supplies a guarantor with a specific obligation.
Before Joseph, Judah says he became surety for the boy to his father; the guarantor's earlier word remains binding in a later crisis.

row.basis: Judah offers himself in the boy's place
row.note: Judah asks to remain a slave instead of Benjamin, putting his own body behind the guarantee; this makes the commentary's image of a surety standing behind another concrete.
The psalmist asks God to be surety for the servant's good against oppressors; the commentary's kefil image extends here from a human promisor to divine protection.

row.basis: Jesus guarantor of a better covenant
row.note: Jesus is called the guarantor of a better covenant; the commentary's kefil and binding inherited obligation meet in a person who stands behind a covenant.
The speaker recalls that his father taught him to hold fast to words and keep commandments; advice is received and passed on, the commentary's generational chain in miniature.
The address to a child instructs acceptance and patience through humiliation; it joins parental admonition with the precise adversity borne in the commentary's Luqman scene.

row.basis: admonish, support and be patient with all
row.note: Paul asks the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient with everyone; mutual counsel and patience operate together.

row.basis: provoke one another to good works
row.note: The assembly must consider how to stir one another to love and good works; the commentary's mutual charge has an enacted ethical goal.

row.basis: keep assembling and encourage one another
row.note: Believers are told to encourage one another as the day approaches; counsel is repeated communally under awareness of limited time.

row.basis: entrust teaching to teachers of others
row.note: What Timothy heard before witnesses is to be entrusted to faithful people able to teach others; testimony, faithful custody and another generation of speakers coincide.
Timothy is told to guard an entrusted good deposit through the Holy Spirit; the commentary's bequeathed instruction is explicitly treated as something in custody.

row.basis: Paul's farewell entrusts elders to God
row.note: In his farewell Paul commends the elders to God and the word able to give inheritance; the departing speaker hands over care and names a future inheritance.
Expecting his departure, the writer promises to enable continued remembrance afterward; instruction deliberately survives the speaker's death.
The argument says a testament requires the death of its maker; it places the commentary's deathbed transfer of binding words beside an explicit death and inheritance analogy.
The next verse says a testament becomes effective on death; it specifies the moment at which a speaker's word binds the living.
Christ mediates a new covenant so the called receive the promised eternal inheritance; the bequest image is used for a religious promise rather than divided property.

row.basis: farewell command to love one another
row.note: At the farewell meal Jesus gives a new command to love one another; a departing teacher leaves a reciprocal obligation to his community.
Abraham trusts the Lord and it is reckoned to him as righteousness; the table's אמנ correspondence links the commentary's faith to a patriarchal act with ethical standing.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; trust and firmness
row.note: Isaiah warns that if the addressed king and house do not trust, they will not stand firm; the verse plays on אמנ twice, making steadfastness the practical stake of belief.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; fidelity through crisis
row.note: The righteous lives by faithfulness while facing the proud oppressor; Hebrew אֱמוּנָה from the table connects the commentary's belief with endurance under strain.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; child asks about statutes
row.note: A child asks what the Lord's decrees mean, prompting parental explanation; חֻקִּים from the table's חקק correspondence turns prescribed right into transmitted teaching.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; decree to Jacob
row.note: God confirms the promise to Jacob as a statute and enduring covenant; Hebrew חֹק from the table's חקק correspondence joins fixed obligation to the patriarchal chain.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; enduring inscribed words
row.note: Job wishes his words written and inscribed in a book; the table's חקק verb gives a concrete form to the commentary's word left behind, though Job seeks a record of his protest rather than an heir's instruction.

The rabbinic account has the dying Jacob fear a fault in his sons, who answer with the Shema; it turns the patriarch's final exchange into the very question of inherited worship developed from Qur'an 2:133.

row.basis: Jacob's final blessings interpreted as faith
row.note: Hebrews describes Jacob's blessing of Joseph's sons as an act of faith at death; it interprets the deathbed transfer as trust in a future he will not see.

row.basis: Joseph's dying charge interpreted as faith
row.note: Hebrews interprets Joseph's instruction about his bones and Israel's exodus at death as an act of faith; it makes the generational obligation depend on confidence in a future event.

row.basis: faith inherited from grandmother and mother
row.note: Timothy's sincere faith is remembered as having lived first in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice; this is a named household chain for the commentary's bequeathed belief.

row.basis: death interrupts plans for stored goods
row.note: God tells a man his life is required that night and asks who will own what he prepared; the commentary's warning that one may lose the chance to leave a bequest becomes an explicit question about successors.
With Moses' death near, he is told to summon Joshua for a charge; it gives the commentary's instruction across a departing generation a named successor.

row.basis: Joshua told to be strong and courageous
row.note: Joshua receives a charge to lead Israel into the land and not lose courage; fortitude accompanies a transferred task, close to the commentary's counsel joined with sabr.

row.basis: choose whom your household will serve
row.note: Joshua sets before Israel a choice of whom to serve and declares his household's allegiance; this is a public answer to the commentary's question of worship after a leader departs.

row.basis: covenant oath not limited to hearers
row.note: Moses explicitly says he makes the covenant and oath with more than the immediate audience; this frames the inherited religious obligation as publicly sworn.
Moses names both those standing there and those not present; the commentary's charge passing beyond its immediate hearers has a precise covenantal counterpart.
A child is told to keep a father's command and not forsake a mother's teaching; this supports the commentary's practical definition of advice as instruction to act.
A good person leaves an inheritance to grandchildren; the commentary's tangible shares and generational gift are joined in one maxim.
Abraham gives all he has to Isaac; the patriarchal transmission of faith in the commentary also has an explicit material inheritance in Genesis.

row.basis: gifts to other sons during life
row.note: Abraham gives gifts to concubines' sons during his life and sends them away from Isaac; the verse shows how a living father distinguishes gifts from the main inheritance.
Reuben offers his sons as a guarantee for Benjamin's return; before Judah's surety, the Genesis Joseph story offers a stark alternate form of standing behind another.
A parent warns a son against pledging himself for a neighbor or stranger; it makes the guarantor's moral exposure explicit where the commentary names the kefil.
The proverb warns that one who guarantees a stranger suffers, while refusal is secure; it supplies the risk implicit in the commentary's surety image.
The Spirit is called a pledge of believers' inheritance until redemption; an assurance stands behind a promised future possession, connecting guarantor and bequest.
God gives the Spirit in hearts as a pledge; the promise is secured before fulfillment, analogous to the commentary's guarantor standing behind a future delivery.

The younger son asks for his share and the father divides his property between them; it supplies a narrative test case for the commentary's distinction between a living father's gift and inherited portions.
The father tells the elder son that all he has is his; even after the younger son has spent his portion, the remaining heir's claim is explicitly preserved.
The sage advises assigning the inheritance at the end of life; this specifies the commentary's moment when a living person's control becomes a charge to heirs.

Amid reflection on life's brevity, a person heaps up wealth without knowing who will gather it; this sharpens the commentary's concern to assign goods before death. Hebrew צבר here means heap, not Arabic sabr's patience.
A wicked person heaps silver and stores clothing, but the following verse assigns them to others; the commentary's estate can outlast the owner without preserving the owner's intended control.
The righteous will wear the stored clothing and the innocent divide the silver; this reverses the accumulator's claim to determine who receives his goods.
Jesus instructs his hearers not to swear at all; the commentary's bequest witnesses are required to swear, so the texts put a different weight on compelled truth telling.
James forbids oaths and requires an unambiguous yes or no; the commentary's oath secures disputed bequest testimony by a legal act that James tells his audience to avoid.
The high priest adjures the detained Jesus by the living God to answer, and Jesus has been silent; a compelled religious oath appears in an interrogation, unlike the commentary's estate witnesses.

row.basis: two or three witnesses establish a matter
row.note: Jesus cites the two or three witness rule when a private rebuke fails; the commentary's disputed testimony likewise requires a claim to be publicly established.
An accusation against an elder is not received without two or three witnesses; the procedure shows why an initial claim needs independently accountable testimony.
A person asks Jesus to tell a brother to divide an inheritance; the commentary's regulated heirs' shares are here voiced as a contested family demand.
Jesus warns the disputants against greed and says life does not consist in possessions; the estate scene adds a moral check on the commentary's concern for rightful shares.
Paul asks believers to encourage and build each other up, and the next exhortation specifies patience with all; this is a communal pattern of mutual counsel.
The community is to let Christ's word dwell richly and teach and admonish one another; a received word is actively passed among peers.
Humility and patience are expressed by bearing with one another in love; the commentary's mutual recommendation of sabr is lived as responsibility for others.
The community is to speak truth in love so the body grows; truth becomes a reciprocal act rather than a private possession.
Timothy is charged to reprove, rebuke and exhort with complete patience and teaching; the commentary's linked counsel and endurance are applied to instruction.
Paul describes himself as being poured out and his departure near; the surrounding charge to Timothy becomes a deliberate word handed on before death.

row.basis: writer expects to lay aside his body
row.note: The writer says his bodily dwelling will soon be put off, immediately before promising enduring remembrance; the bequest of teaching is motivated by expected death.
Believers are told to stand firm and hold traditions taught orally or by letter; the commentary's inherited charge is preserved in two concrete channels.

row.basis: faith handed over once for all
row.note: Jude urges a community to contend for the faith entrusted to the saints; a received deposit calls for continued action by those who inherit it.
At the final meal Jesus calls the cup the new covenant in his blood; a departing speaker leaves a binding religious relation to his followers.
Jesus says when giving alms, do not display it for praise; beside the commentary's Qur'anic Jesus commanded to give alms, the Gospel describes how his hearers should give.
Jesus says when praying, do not perform it for spectators; beside the commentary's Qur'anic Jesus commanded to pray, the Gospel passes prayer instruction to hearers.
Cornelius is told his prayers and alms have ascended before God; the two practices paired in the commentary's speech of Jesus are joined in a remembered disciple's life.
Jesus answers a disciple's request by giving words to pray; the Qur'anic command laid on Jesus becomes a practice he hands to his followers in this scene.
God warns Israel and Judah through every prophet and seer to turn back and keep his commandments; it gives concrete precedent for the commentary's one charge passing through messengers.

row.basis: God speaks through prophets across generations
row.note: God formerly spoke to the ancestors by prophets in many ways; it parallels the commentary's continuous chain of divine instruction to successive messengers.

row.basis: God speaks in the Son in last days
row.note: The following verse presents speech through the Son in the last days; it marks a specifically Christian culmination beside the commentary's sequence from Noah to Jesus.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; supported hands stay steady
row.note: Others support Moses' hands until sunset, and they remain אֱמוּנָה, steady; the table's אמנ family makes firmness a supported communal action beside the commentary's faith and patience.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; faithful covenant keeper
row.note: God is called faithful and keeps covenant and loyalty with those who love and obey him to a thousand generations; the table's אמנ family joins trustworthiness to a long inherited obligation.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; faithful covenant promise
row.note: God says his steadfast love will not be removed or his faithfulness made false; אֱמוּנָה from the table's אמנ field marks the reliability of a promise continuing to descendants.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; statutes and descendants
row.note: Israel must keep God's statutes so that it goes well with them and their children after them; the table's חקק correspondence joins prescribed duty to the commentary's bequest across generations.
The Passover day is to be kept as a statute through generations; Hebrew חֻקָּה from the table's חקק correspondence makes a binding inherited instruction into a recurring act.

row.basis: hope in God and keep commandments
row.note: The purpose of telling children is that they set hope in God, remember his works and keep his commands; transmitted faith and action are both named.

row.basis: Jacob promises God will accompany sons
row.note: As death nears Jacob says God will be with his sons and bring them back to their fathers' land; the parting word carries a future promise beyond the father's life.
A person who vows to the Lord or binds himself by oath must not break his word but do what he said; the commentary's binding testament and weighty oath meet in the force of an utterance.

row.basis: parental teaching addressed to a son
row.note: A son is instructed to hear his father's discipline and not abandon his mother's teaching; the form of address matches the commentary's Luqman instructing his son.

row.basis: wait patiently and keep the way
row.note: The psalm calls its hearer to wait for the Lord and keep his way amid the wicked's apparent success; obedience and endurance are joined as in the commentary's final counsel.
James points to prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience; it unites the commentary's messenger chain with the sabr expected of those who inherit their charge.
The community is told it has heard of Job's endurance and seen the Lord's outcome; endurance is transmitted as a remembered example to later hearers.

row.basis: people do not know their time
row.note: Like fish in a net and birds in a snare, people are caught by sudden calamity; it makes concrete the commentary's warning that death may arrive before a bequest can be made.

Jesus tells disciples to be ready because the Son of Man comes at an unexpected hour; this is an indirect analogue to the commentary's people overtaken before they can leave an instruction, although the verse concerns the Son of Man's coming.

row.basis: plea for someone to be surety
row.note: Job asks God for a pledge and who will give surety for him; the legal image resembles the commentary's kefil, though Job's disputed standing before God differs from Joseph's announced reward.

row.basis: Monica's final request to her sons
row.note: Near death Monica asks her sons to remember her at the Lord's altar; this is a Christian example of a dying parent's religious charge, though it concerns memorial prayer rather than inheritance or a sworn witness.
Joshua is told to be strong and carefully do all the law Moses commanded him; a successor receives both an actionable charge and the endurance needed to carry it out.

row.basis: command children to obey all the words
row.note: Moses tells Israel to set its heart on his warning and command its children to observe the law; the dying generation actively passes an obligation to the next.

row.basis: David charges Solomon to know his father's God
row.note: David tells his son Solomon to know the God of his father and serve him wholeheartedly; the commentary's inherited worship and practical instruction meet in a father's direct charge.

row.basis: aged speaker tells the next generation
row.note: The aged psalmist asks not to be forsaken until he has declared God's power to the next generation; an approaching end makes transmission of testimony urgent.
The Rechabites refuse wine because their ancestor Jonadab commanded them and their children never to drink it; a concrete instruction continues after its speaker's death.

row.basis: Jonadab's words observed to this day
row.note: God cites the Rechabites' continuing obedience to their ancestor's instruction as a rebuke to Judah's failure to heed repeated divine speech; inherited counsel becomes a measure of faithfulness.
The law treats deception over a neighbor's deposited goods as a breach against the Lord; it gives moral and legal weight to the commentary's emanet left in another's keeping. This uses WLC numbering.

The same law names finding lost property, denying it and swearing falsely; the commentary's suspicion of corrupt sworn testimony concerns an equally concrete property dispute. This uses WLC numbering.
Laban tells Jacob that if he mistreats Laban's daughters, God is witness even with no human observer; a father's concern for descendants is secured by testimony beyond his presence.

row.basis: oath honored even at personal cost
row.note: The person fit to dwell with God swears to his own hurt and does not change his word; it clarifies the weight of the commentary's binding oath when keeping it becomes burdensome.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; believer does not hurry
row.note: The one who trusts the tested cornerstone will not hurry in panic; Hebrew אמנ from the table joins believing with a concrete form of patient steadiness.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; trust and be established
row.note: Jehoshaphat tells Judah to trust the Lord and be established, then trust his prophets and prosper; the verse repeats אמנ and links firm faith to heeding a transmitted prophetic word.
Isaiah condemns those who decree oppressive decrees; Hebrew חקק from the table shows that a binding rule can itself be unjust, sharpening the commentary's concern about an unfair will.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; forgetting decree harms rights
row.note: A king who drinks may forget what is decreed and distort the poor person's legal claim; Hebrew חקק from the table puts prescribed law and vulnerable claimants in the same maternal admonition.
The rabbinic chain has Moses receive Torah and hand it to Joshua, then elders, prophets and the Great Assembly; it interprets religious instruction as an inherited trust across successive speakers.

row.basis: dying father's instructions to his son
row.note: Believing he may die, Tobit calls Tobias and charges him to bury him and care for his mother; a dying speaker gives a son concrete duties to perform afterward.
Paul asks Philemon to charge to him anything Onesimus owes or any wrong he has done; he personally stands behind another's liability like the commentary's kefil.

row.basis: Paul writes his promise to repay
row.note: Paul writes with his own hand that he will repay Onesimus's debt; the guarantor's undertaking becomes an explicit, durable promise.

row.basis: continue in learning received from others
row.note: Timothy is told to continue in what he learned, knowing the people from whom he learned it; the received charge depends on identifiable transmitters and continued practice.
Timothy has known the sacred writings from infancy, and they can make him wise for salvation; the inherited word is a specific text learned before adulthood.

row.basis: what Paul received he handed on
row.note: Paul explicitly says he handed to the Corinthians what he received about the Lord's final meal; a departing speaker's act becomes a repeated communal instruction.
Paul says he handed on as first importance what he received, beginning with Christ's death for sins; belief is carried by a deliberate chain of testimony.
Jesus prays at his farewell for people who will believe through his disciples' word; his instruction moves beyond those present to a future generation.
Readers are to remember the words spoken by holy prophets and the Lord's command through apostles; the charge crosses a chain of messengers and remains active in its hearers.

row.basis: teach children fear of God from youth
row.note: The community's instruction tells parents to teach sons and daughters reverence for God from childhood; the inherited religious charge is made a household duty.

row.basis: Joshua speaks as his death nears
row.note: Joshua says he is going the way of all the earth and reminds Israel that God's promises have not failed; a leader's last speech preserves a standard for successors.
David tells Solomon he will prosper if he observes the statutes given through Moses and urges him to be strong, courageous and unafraid; inherited law is paired with fortitude.
Moses says the commanded word is no empty thing but Israel's life, by which their days in the land will be prolonged; the inherited counsel has an explicitly future consequence.

A dispute over an animal, garment or lost article is brought by both parties before God for judgment; this supplies a procedure when a custodian's claim about entrusted property is contested. This uses WLC numbering.

The wrongdoer must restore the property in full and add a fifth when guilt is acknowledged; the commentary's correction of an unjust transfer has a concrete restitution analogue. This uses WLC numbering.

row.basis: speak truth and judge for peace
row.note: People are told to speak truth to one another and render truthful judgments that make for peace; mutual truth telling has the restorative legal effect sought when a bequest is disputed.

row.basis: false oath rejected with harmful intent
row.note: The next instruction rejects plotting harm against a neighbor and loving a false oath; the commentary's contested witnesses unite the same dangers of malice and sworn deception.
Israel is forbidden to spread a false report or join a wicked person as a malicious witness; the rule addresses collusion behind the commentary's suspect testimony.
The proverb forbids becoming a witness against a neighbor without cause and deceiving with one's lips; it spells out the ethical fault when legal testimony is manufactured.
The sage praises becoming surety for a neighbor while contrasting it with a shameless person's failure to do so; it supplies a Jewish ethical valuation of the commentary's kefil.
The beneficiary is warned not to forget a guarantor who has exposed himself for another; the commentary's surety carries a personal cost beyond merely announcing a pledge.
The sage says it is better for children to seek from a living parent than for that parent to depend on them; this qualifies the commentary's image of a father trying to retrieve a gift already made.

row.basis: Joseph stores grain for future need
row.note: Joseph directs grain to be collected under Pharaoh for the coming famine; this supplies the food administration behind the Joseph story's promised load of grain, independently of Hebrew צבר, whose heaping sense is unrelated to Arabic sabr.

row.basis: prophet entrusts his words to a scribe
row.note: Baruch writes the words Jeremiah dictates on a scroll; the commentary's advice passed to another to act becomes a specific transfer of a prophet's speech.

row.basis: restrained speaker must use a delegate
row.note: Jeremiah says he is barred from entering the Lord's house, so Baruch must carry and read the message; a speaker's inability to act makes a successor's faithful performance necessary.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; decree given to a son
row.note: The king recites the Lord's decree declaring him a son; Hebrew חֹק from the table connects a prescribed word to a father-son relation, though it is a royal oracle rather than an inheritance allotment.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; unfaithful covenant hearers
row.note: The generation instructed about God's deeds is said to be unfaithful to his covenant; Hebrew אמנ from the table supplies the contrary case to the commentary's inherited faithfulness.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; Abraham's faithful heart
row.note: The prayer says God found Abraham's heart faithful and made covenant with him; the table's אמנ family joins the patriarch's trust to a promise carried to descendants.

row.basis: unjust decrees dispossess widows and orphans
row.note: The continuation says the decrees deprive the needy of justice and make widows and orphans prey; it specifies whose rights are injured when prescribed allocations are corrupted.
Paul says he writes to admonish the Corinthians as beloved children; spiritual parenthood supplies the commentary's personal relation between adviser and heir.
Paul sends Timothy to remind the Corinthians of his ways in Christ, as he teaches in every church; a recipient of instruction becomes its bearer to another group.

row.basis: practice what was learned and received
row.note: Paul asks believers to put into practice what they learned, received, heard and saw in him; the inherited word includes conduct for its recipients to enact.

row.basis: parents bring children up in admonition
row.note: Fathers are told to raise children in the Lord's discipline and instruction; household advice is a sustained responsibility, as in the commentary's father-to-child counsel.
Paul says destructive wolves will enter after he leaves; the farewell charge anticipates dangers the recipients must meet when the original speaker is gone.
Paul tells elders to stay alert and remember that he admonished each with tears for three years; the departing teacher leaves a remembered practice of warning.
The writer intends to keep reminding hearers even though they know and are established in the truth; repeated counsel protects what will remain after his departure.

row.basis: two or three witnesses in apostolic dispute
row.note: Paul invokes the rule that a matter is established by two or three witnesses before his next visit; the commentary's bequest dispute likewise requires accountable plurality in testimony.
Jesus cites the legal rule that the testimony of two people is true while defending his own witness; the estate-witness formula is reused in a different dispute over credibility.
Jesus says he bears witness and the Father who sent him also bears witness; the preceding two-witness rule is given an unusual father-son application.
